transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Democrats will take control of the House in January,
leaving the GOP to regroup in the minority.
House Republicans have chosen Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan
over Louisiana Congressman Steve Scalise to lead them in the new Congress.
NPR's Barbara Spunt reports the outcome signals how Republicans want to move forward
following last week's election losses.
This election is sort of a choice between continuity and change.
Jordan is certainly the change candidate.
He's the co-founder of the Ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus,
which as we all know was often a thorn in the side of Republican leadership.
Scalise is seen as more of a moderate, an extension of that leadership era of Johnson.
And so the vote tells me that House Republicans wanted a clean break from that leadership era.
I think folks are craving a new chapter after their massive loss last week.
That's NPR's Barbara Spunt reporting.
A new federal rule requiring Americans and certain immigrants to verify their eligibility
could evict tens of thousands of people from public housing,
including many U.S. citizen children.
NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports the measure targets families with mixed immigration status.
Immigrants in the U.S. unlawfully do not get federal rental aid,
but since the '90s, Congress has let them live with family members who do.
Housing Secretary Scott Turner calls that "exploiting a loophole"
and says it's not fair to U.S. citizens,
especially since rental aid is deeply underfunded
and only a quarter of those eligible ever get it.
Housing advocates and other critics say the new rule could separate families
and will actually cost more.
That's because mixed-status households get a smaller subsidy than those where every member is eligible.
In its own analysis, the federal housing agency says that will mean the same budget will help fewer people.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
It's day three of the United Nations' COP 31 climate summit in Turkey.
NPR's Hadil al-Shalci reports curbing climate change has been a major focus of the conference.
World leaders will join Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Antalya today
to discuss ways that countries can fight global warming.
They include the Iranian president, the Australian prime minister, and the U.N. secretary-general.
The talks come during a tumultuous year when global oil prices have risen due to the war with Iran,
forcing some countries to rethink how they use energy.
The U.N. says global warming will surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit
and developing nations receive barely a fraction of the $300 billion the U.N. says they need to adapt to climate change.
The U.S. will be absent from the summit for a second year in a row
and is set to soon leave the larger framework that organizes international climate negotiations.
Hadil al-Shalci, NPR News, Antalya.
This is NPR News in Washington.
The number of Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 11,000,
making it the deadliest outbreak in the country.
More than 5,300 people have died since May.
Armed conflict and struggling health system have hampered efforts to contain the virus.
As many Americans prepare to drive long distances for the upcoming holidays,
a new report for the National Sleep Foundation finds many are driving dangerously drowsy.
Scott Massione from member station WYPR has more on how to stay safe.
About 61 percent of drivers admit to driving while feeling sleepy, according to the new study.
Drowsy driving is responsible for about 20 percent of deadly vehicle accidents in the United States.
The report from the National Sleep Foundation also says many people don't recognize warning signs
of driving while impaired from tiredness.
Sleep experts say frequent blinking or yawning is one of the first indicators someone shouldn't be behind the wheel.
Trouble keeping eyes open, nodding off or drifting from lanes are clear signs that it's time to pull over.
For NPR News, I'm Scott Massione in Baltimore.
An ocean liner that once set a transatlantic speed record is headed for a new role
as the world's largest artificial reef.
Florida officials have begun the process of sinking the SSS United States
in the Gulf off the coast of Destin.
Crews will remove materials that could harm the environment while preserving much of the ship's structure.
The historic liner set its speed record on its maiden voyage in 1952.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: House Republicans choose Jim Jordan over Steve Scalise to lead the new Congress
New federal rule could evict tens of thousands from public housing, including citizen children
COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, opens with world leaders discussing global warming
Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo surpass 11,000, deadliest outbreak in the country
National Sleep Foundation report finds many drivers drive drowsy ahead of holiday travel
Florida begins sinking the SS United States off Destin to create world's largest artificial reef
